title: Arrays Basics

steps.title: What is an Array?
steps.content: An array is a collection of elements of the same type stored at contiguous memory locations. Each element is accessed by its index (position).
steps.example: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]. arr[0] = 10, arr[2] = 30. Indexing starts at 0.
steps.tip: Array access is O(1) — instant. But insertion/deletion in the middle is O(n) because elements must shift.

steps.title: Access Elements
steps.explanation: arr[3] accesses the element at index 3, which is the 4th element: 20. Remember: indexing starts at 0.

steps.title: Array Traversal
steps.prompt: What is the time complexity of traversing all elements of an array of size n?
steps.explanation: We must visit each element exactly once, so the time complexity is O(n).

steps.title: Common Array Operations
steps.content: Common operations: Search (O(n) linear, O(log n) binary if sorted), Insert at end (O(1) amortized), Insert in middle (O(n) due to shifting), Delete from middle (O(n) due to shifting).
steps.example: Inserting at index 2 in [1, 2, 3, 4] requires shifting elements at indices 2 and 3 rightward: [1, 2, new, 3, 4].

steps.title: Two-Pointer Preview
steps.prompt: To find if a pair of numbers in a sorted array sums to a target, which technique is most efficient?
steps.explanation: Two pointers (left at start, right at end) can find a pair in O(n) for sorted arrays. Move left pointer forward if sum < target, right pointer backward if sum > target.

steps.title: Predict an array update
steps.content: Trace the values after the assignment before calculating the final expression.
steps.explanation: The middle element changes from 7 to 5. The sum is 4 + 5 + 2 = 11.

steps.title: Trace a safe array traversal
steps.content: A loop that visits every array element must check its index before reading the element and increment after processing.
steps.prompt: Put these operations in the correct order for a forward traversal.
options: Process the element at the current index
Check that the index is less than the array length
steps.explanation: Start at index 0, check that it is within the array, process that element, then increment. The next iteration checks the new index before accessing it.

steps.title: Find the largest value
steps.content: The first value is a useful starting candidate. Scan the remaining values and replace the candidate whenever you find a larger value.
steps.prompt: Complete the comparison so the program prints the largest value: 19.
hints: Compare scores[index] with the current largest value.
Only replace largest when the current array value is greater.
Assign scores[index] to largest inside that condition.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in an array?
questions.explanation: Array access by index is O(1) because the memory address is calculated directly: base_address + index × element_size.

questions.prompt: Which operation is most expensive on an array?
questions.explanation: Inserting in the middle requires shifting all subsequent elements, making it O(n). Accessing first/last elements and updating are O(1).

questions.prompt: Which index refers to the last element of an array containing n elements?
questions.explanation: With zero-based indexing, valid indices run from 0 through n - 1.

questions.prompt: You need to find the largest number in an unsorted array. What is the best general approach?
options: Scan every value while tracking the largest
questions.explanation: A single scan takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Binary search requires sorted data.

questions.prompt: Why can inserting an item at the beginning of a fixed-size contiguous array take O(n) time?
options: Existing elements may need to shift right
questions.explanation: To make room at the beginning, all existing elements may need to move one position.

srs_cards.question: What is the time complexity of array operations: access, insert at end, insert in middle, delete from middle?
srs_cards.answer: Access: O(1), insert at end: O(1) amortized, insert in middle: O(n), delete from middle: O(n).

srs_cards.question: For an array of length n, what are the first and last valid indices?
Why is a full array traversal O(n)?
srs_cards.answer: The algorithm performs a constant amount of work for each of n elements.

srs_cards.question: When is the inward two-pointer pair-sum method appropriate?
srs_cards.answer: When the input is sorted, or has been sorted while accounting for the sorting cost.

learning_objectives: Explain what an array stores and how zero-based indexing works.
Trace reads and updates without confusing an index with a position.
Choose between linear search, sorting, and two pointers for a simple problem.
Explain the time cost of access, traversal, insertion, and deletion.
Implement a safe traversal and find the minimum or maximum value.

common_misconceptions.correction: Indexing starts at zero, so index 3 is the fourth element.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Reading an array element always scans the array.
common_misconceptions.correction: An array can calculate an indexed element's address directly, so indexed access is O(1).

common_misconceptions.misconception: Insertion in the middle is O(1).
common_misconceptions.correction: Elements after the insertion point usually need to shift, making it O(n).

common_misconceptions.misconception: Two pointers works on every unsorted pair-sum input.
common_misconceptions.correction: The simple inward-moving two-pointer method relies on sorted order.
